study.title: Numbers 36 - Preserved heritage among tribes
study.overview: The chapter closes the question of the daughters of Zelophehad by showing how the Lord protected the righteousness given to them and the integrity of Israel's tribal inheritance. The heads of the Manasseh family lead Moses a practical concern: if these heiress marry outside the tribe, the portion received by their family may pass to another tribe. The divine response confirms the request, but establishes a rule: they can marry freely, as long as they remain within their father's family. Thus, the chapter unites right, prudence, and obedience, concluding with the assertion that these commandments were given through Moses in the fields of Moab, at the gates of entry into Canaan.

outline.title: The concern of the chiefs of Manasseh
outline.explanation: The leaders of Gilead's family expose to Moses a concrete problem linked to the inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad. The jubilee would not solve this transfer, because the case is not of land sold, but of inheritance linked to marriage. The concern is to preserve the portion of the tribe without denying the right granted to daughters.

outline.title: The Lord's decision on marriage and inheritance
outline.explanation: Moses declares that the tribe of Joseph spoke correctly and presents the determination of the LORD: the heiress can marry whom they desire, but within the family of the tribe of his father. The purpose is to prevent the inheritance from passing tribe into tribe and keeping each tribe linked to its portion received.

outline.title: Obedience of daughters and closing of the book
outline.explanation: The five daughters obey and marry the sons of their uncles, preserving the inheritance in the tribe of Manasseh. The chapter ends with the final formula that summarizes the commandments and statutes given by the LORD through Moses in the fields of Moab.

study.context: The text is located in the fields of Moab, near the Jordan of Jericho, in the final period of the journey of Israel before the entrance to Canaan. The chapter itself is presented as a conclusion of a series of commandments given to the people. The notes also report that the question of the daughters of Zelofeade had already been dealt with previously in Numbers 27, and that the consequences of this decision for the organization of the tribes and their inheritances are now examined.
study.theology: The chapter shows that God's justice is not abstract: it deals with concrete cases and seeks to preserve the good of real people without breaking the order of the covenant. There is an important balance here between mercy and government: the Lord grants inheritance to the daughters, but it also protects the tribal structure given to Israel. Obedience appears as a proper response to the divine word, and the inheritance is not only treated as material possession, but as a responsibility received from God and linked to the identity of the people. It is also seen that human freedom is real, but guided by holy limits: they could choose a husband, but not in a way to harm the portion inherited by the family. This combination of care, order and submission highlights that the life of God's people must be organized according to the will of the Lord, without injustice or disorder.

scholarViews.insight: The daughters who inherited land could, when marrying outside the tribe, cause the inheritance to come out of the ancestral lineage; therefore, the rule was given to avoid this transfer.
The petition of the tribe of Manasseh is received with approval; God not only directs what to do, but also welcomes the search for his will.
The chapter shows a prudent arrangement: the heiresers maintain freedom of choice, but with a healthy restriction to prevent the inconvenient mixture of possession and inheritance.

questions: How does this chapter help to understand what justice and order can walk together in God's people?
What aspects of the freedom of the daughters of Zelophehad are preserved, and what limits are established?
How does their obedience serve as an example for family and community decisions today?
study.practice: This chapter invites you to seek decisions that honor God's righteousness without prejudice to others or the community of faith. In practice, this means evaluating personal, family and financial choices in the light of spiritual responsibility, and not just individual interest. He also teaches to obey promptly when the will of the Lord is enlightened, entrusting that his limits are wise and good. Instead of seeing biblical rules as mere restrictions, the reader is led to see them as means of preserving the good received from God.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain in detail how this norm was applied in cases other than the example of Zelophehad's daughters. The notes suggest relations with the previous legislation and the jubilee, but the exact extent of its historical application is not fully developed here. It is also not possible to affirm, from this chapter alone, all subsequent developments of this regulation.
